I at least want to connect those, but right now I just tie a knot which is not optimal. I could at least wrap it around a hook or something
turns.response_html:
You are staring down the classic evolution of shade design. Moving from a manual tie-off to a unified, smooth mechanical system is incredibly satisfying.

To tackle all three goals—smoother pull, a single unified cord, and no more manual knots—you can look directly at how industrial blinds work, but build it with a custom DIY spin.

1. Unifying the Strings (The Cable Harness)

Right now, you have a left string and a right string. Pulling two distinct strings at identical rates to keep the curtain level is a hassle.

Instead of routing both strings all the way down to your hand, you want to combine them at the top corner of the window frame.

  • The Set up: * String A (Far side): Runs up through the curtain, hits a smooth turning point at the top-left, travels horizontally across the top frame to the top-right corner, and drops down.
    • String B (Near side): Runs up through the curtain, hits a turning point at the top-right corner, and immediately drops down alongside String A.
  • The Join: Tie String A and String B together into a single knot just below the top-right turning point. From that knot down, attach a single, thicker, more comfortable pull-cord.

2. Making the Pull Smoother (Friction Reduction)

To make the pull effortless, you need to replace fabric or sharp frame edges with low-friction turning points.

  • Low-Fi Option (Screw Eyes): Smooth metal screw-eye hooks work remarkably well if the string is slick (like nylon paracord or braided line).
  • Mid-Fi Option (Bowden Tubes / PEX): If you want to route the strings cleanly along the frame without wheels, you can use short segments of PTFE (Teflon) tubing or even PEX pipe as smooth, curved guide channels. String slides through PTFE with almost zero friction.
  • High-Fi Option (Pulley Wheels): If you want to use small wheels, look into micro-pulleys or small bearing wheels designed for 3D printers or window screens. You can mount these at the top corners of the frame.

3. Eliminating the Knot (Locking Mechanisms)

Tying a knot every time is the biggest bottleneck. Here are three ways to upgrade, ranging from a simple hook to fully automatic:

Option A: The Awning Cleat (Easiest / Cleanest)

Instead of tying a complex knot, screw a small zigzag cleat or boat cleat into the wall or frame.

  • How it works: You just pull the unified cord down, wrap it around the cleat in a figure-eight pattern twice, and friction holds it instantly. No knots, just a 2-second wrap.

Option B: The Cord Lock (Like a Backpack Toggle)

You can source a heavy-duty spring-loaded cord lock (the kind found on backpacks or hoodies) or a mechanical cord lock used in actual Roman shades.

  • How it works: Thread the unified cord through the spring lock. When you pull the curtain up, slide the toggle up against a fixed anchor hook on the frame to lock it in place.

Option C: The Gravity Cam Lock (Automatic)

If you want the "pull to the side to lock" action of standard commercial blinds, you need a small cam-cleat or a gravity roller shade lock mounted at the top-right corner where the cords drop.

  • How it works: It uses a small ridged wheel or wedge. When you pull the cord straight down, it moves freely. When you swing the cord to the side and let go slightly, the wedge pinches the cord against the housing, locking it automatically.

The Blueprint For Your Next Iteration

A highly reliable, satisfying setup would look like this:

  1. Mount two low-friction turning points (smooth screw eyes or micro-pulleys) at the top corners of your window frame.
  2. Route the left string across the top to meet the right string at the right-hand pulley.
  3. Tie them together into a single pull-cord just past that right pulley.
  4. Mount an awning cleat or a spring-loaded toggle on the wall at chest height to secure the single cord instantly.

Which of these locking mechanisms matches the aesthetic and effort level you're aiming for?

turns.prompt_text: The Roman shade sounds pretty cool. I would essentially just have to put in a pole at the bottom of each one and they have a snug pocket for that already built in. They just don't have the solid pole. It'd be interesting if I could automate it like put in some sort of gear mechanism with a motor
turns.response_html:
Replacing the soft weight at the bottom with a rigid pole (like a wood dowel, aluminum rod, or PVC pipe) is a major upgrade. It distributes the weight evenly across the entire width of the fabric, ensuring it pulls up in clean, straight horizontal folds rather than bunching up toward the center.

Since you are already thinking about a rigid bottom bar and a smooth pull system, transitioning this into an automated, motorized setup is highly doable.

The Mechanical Layout

For automation, instead of pulling a cord by hand, you shift to a rotational spool system located at the top of the window frame.

  • The Top Axle (The Drive Shaft): You mount a single rotating rod or axle across the top of the window frame.
  • The Take-up Spools: Fixed onto this top axle are two small spools (one aligned with each vertical string line). The tops of your curtain strings tie directly to these spools.
  • How it works: When the motor spins the top axle, both spools turn at the exact same rate, winding the strings up evenly and lifting the curtain bottom bar straight up. When the motor reverses, gravity drops the curtain back down.

3 Ways to Motorize It

Depending on how much custom control you want, there are a few standard engineering approaches to powering the drive shaft:

1. The Continuous Servo (Easiest Software Control)

Using a 360-degree continuous rotation servo motor is a fantastic entry point.

  • The Gear Setup: You can attach a small drive gear directly to the servo horn, which meshes with a larger gear fixed to your top axle (giving you mechanical advantage/torque).
  • The Benefit: Servos have built-in motor drivers and H-bridges. You don't need external motor controllers; you just feed it a standard PWM signal from a microcontroller to control direction and speed.

2. Geared DC Motor with Limit Switches (High Torque)

A standard yellow hobby gearmotor or a small metal DC gearmotor provides excellent torque to lift heavier fabric and a solid bottom bar.

  • The Control: You’ll need an external H-bridge circuit (like an L298N or a simple dual-MOSFET driver) to reverse the polarity and change direction.
  • The Trap: DC motors don't know where they are. To prevent the motor from ripping the strings out when it reaches the top or bottom, you mount tiny physical limit switches at the top of the frame. When the rigid bottom bar hits the switch, it cuts power to the motor circuit.

3. Stepper Motor (Precision & No Switches)

A small stepper motor (like a NEMA 17) gives you perfect precision without needing limit switches.

  • The Control: By driving it with a dedicated stepper driver, you can program the exact number of steps it takes to go from fully deployed to fully raised.
  • The Benefit: It holds its position firmly when stopped, ensuring the curtain doesn't slowly slide back down under its own weight.

Quick Design Tip: Counterweights

Because you’re relying on gravity to lower the curtain, ensure the pole you slip into the bottom pocket has enough mass to overcome the inherent internal friction of your top gear/motor assembly when it's unspooling. If it's too light, the string will go slack at the top while the fabric stays bunched up. Wood dowels are great, but a solid steel or aluminum rod adds that perfect crisp, heavy drop.

Are you leaning toward keeping this a self-contained hardware project using simple switches, or are you thinking about driving it with a microcontroller for smart automation?

There could even be stages where it is connected straight to the gear for lifting. Locked into place so gravity doesn't pull on. Leave your system or Free falling
turns.response_html:
Using a geared DC motor is an excellent choice. Small hobby gearmotors are highly affordable, surprisingly torquey due to internal gear reduction, and incredibly easy to interface with simple switches or custom electronics.

Your idea of a mechanical clutch or shift lever to disengage the drivetrain for a pure gravity drop is a clever engineering approach. It saves you from having to run the motor in reverse just to lower the blinds, and it gives that incredibly satisfying, instant "free-fall" deployment.

To achieve your three distinct stages—Lifting (engaged), Locked (holding), and Free-Falling (disengaged)—you can design a simple manual shifting mechanism.

The 3-Stage Mechanical Design

To make this work, the gear on your motor needs to slide or pivot into different positions relative to the gear on your main curtain axle.

       [Stage 1: LIFT]                 [Stage 2: LOCK]               [Stage 3: FREE FALL]
     
        (Motor Gear)                    (Motor Gear)                    (Motor Gear)
            [O]                             [O]                             [O]
             |                                                               
            [O]=============(X)             [O]=============(X)             [O]             (X)
       (Curtain Gear)   (Lock Pawl)    (Curtain Gear)   (Lock Pawl)    (Curtain Gear)   (Lock Pawl)

Stage 1: The Lift (Engaged)

  • The Mechanism: Your shifting lever pushes the motor assembly forward so its drive gear meshes perfectly with the curtain axle gear.
  • The Action: When you apply power to the DC motor, it spins the axle, winds up the strings, and raises the curtain.

Stage 2: The Lock (Holding Position)

  • The Mechanism: When you turn off the motor, the weight of the curtain will want to back-drive the motor and slip back down. To prevent this without keeping the motor powered on (which would burn it out), your lever shifts into a middle detent.
  • The Action: This shifts the motor gear away from the axle gear, but simultaneously drops a rigid pin or wedge (a lock pawl) into the teeth of the curtain axle gear. The axle is mechanically locked in place, holding the curtain at your desired height.

Stage 3: Free Fall (Disengaged)

  • The Mechanism: You pull the lever all the way back.
  • The Action: This pulls the locking pin out of the axle gear and keeps the motor gear disengaged. With zero friction holding the top axle, the heavy pole in the bottom pocket instantly pulls the strings down, deploying the curtain via pure gravity.

3D Printing & Prototyping the Clutch

Since you need precise geometry for gears and shifting tracks, this is a textbook project for a 3D printer. You can rapidly iterate on the tolerances for the sliding components.

  • Material Choice: Standard PLA is perfectly fine for prototyping the frame and lever, but for the actual gears and the shifting track, PETG or Nylon will handle the repetitive mechanical friction and stress much better without shearing teeth.
  • The Linear Slider: You can design a small modular carrier block for the DC motor that slides along a dedicated linear rail. A simple manual spring-loaded lever can lock the carrier block into three notches cut into the frame (Lift, Lock, Drop).

Pro-Tip for the "Free Fall" Stage

When a curtain free-falls via gravity, it can drop fast. When the heavy bottom pole hits the window sill, the top axle will want to keep spinning due to momentum, which can cause your strings to unspool completely and bird-nest (tangle up) inside your enclosure.

To prevent this, you can add a small friction dampener or a felt pad that lightly presses against the axle during the free-fall stage, slowing the drop just enough to keep tension on the strings, or rely on a rubber bumper at the bottom window sill to absorb the final impact smoothly.

How are you thinking about designing the shifting interface—a manual mechanical lever next to the window, or a soleniod-driven clutch?

turns.prompt_text: I'm thinking of something where I have to press in order to allow the Free Fall to occur and when I release it prevents it from falling further than if the motor activates. It is able to remain in a locked from falling for their state but allows it to pull up. I'm thinking of a ratchet strap gear
turns.response_html:
You have just hit on the exact engineering concept behind the ratchet and pawl mechanism. It is the perfect mechanical solution for this because it natively allows movement in only one direction (lifting) while completely blocking movement in the other direction (falling) until you explicitly press a release lever.

By using a spring-loaded or gravity-assisted pawl against a sawtooth gear, you get the exact user experience you are looking for:

  1. Lifting: The motor spins, the teeth slip right past the pawl (making a satisfying click-click-click sound), and the curtain goes up.
  2. Holding: The moment the motor stops, the pawl jams into the straight edge of the tooth, locking it instantly against gravity.
  3. Free Fall: You press down on a lever attached to the pawl, lifting it completely out of the gear teeth. The axle spins freely, and the curtain drops.
  4. Instant Stop: If you let go of the lever mid-drop, the spring snaps the pawl back into the teeth, arresting the fall immediately.

Designing the Ratchet and Drive System

To combine this with a DC motor, you have to decide how the motor interacts with the ratchet axle. There are two primary ways to design this layout:

Approach A: The Common-Axle (Simplest Geometry)

In this layout, your DC motor is directly coupled to the main curtain axle via a set of gears. The ratchet gear is fixed permanently onto that same axle.

  • How it works: When you want to lift, you turn on the motor. The motor has enough torque to drive the axle upward, forcing the pawl to ride up and over the sloped teeth. When you want to drop the curtain, you press the lever to lift the pawl and you keep the motor circuit open (disengaged electrically) so the weight of the curtain can back-drive the motor's internal gearbox.
  • The Catch: Many DC gearmotors have very high internal gear ratios (like 100:1 or 200:1). This internal friction might prevent a pure, fast gravity "free-fall" because the falling curtain has to force the motor to spin backward at high speed.

Approach B: The One-Way Clutch Bearing (The Elegant Fix)

If you find that the DC motor's internal gearbox blocks the curtain from falling quickly when the pawl is released, you can introduce a one-way needle roller bearing (often called a sprag clutch) between the motor drive gear and the curtain axle.

  • Lifting: When the motor spins forward, the one-way bearing locks up, gripping the axle and driving the curtain upward. The ratchet pawl clicks along.
  • Holding: The motor stops, the bearing unlocks, but the ratchet pawl catches the axle gear, holding the curtain in place.
  • Free Fall: You press the pawl release lever. Because the one-way bearing allows the axle to spin completely freely in the downward direction without forcing the motor's gears to turn, the curtain drops in a true, uninhibited free fall.

3D Printing the Ratchet Mechanism

This is incredibly easy to prototype on your Bambu Lab printer.

  • The Teeth Design: When modeling the ratchet gear, don't use standard symmetric gear teeth. Design them as asymmetric triangles—one side should have a gentle slope (roughly 30° to 45°) for the pawl to slide up smoothly during lifting, and the other side should be a sharp, vertical drop (90° or slightly undercut) to securely trap the pawl.
  • The Spring Return: Instead of trying to source a tiny metal torsion spring for the pawl lever, you can design a compliant mechanism right into your 3D print. Print a thin, curved plastic leaf-spring integrated into the pawl housing out of PETG. PETG has excellent fatigue resistance and elasticity, meaning the plastic itself will act as the spring to snap the pawl back into the gear teeth the second you let go of the button.

Do you want to design the ratchet gear as a standalone component that mounts onto a standard wooden dowel or aluminum rod, or are you thinking about integrating it directly into the spool housing at the top corner?

So essentially I have three curtains in this system. I would prefer if these stay on three independent tracks. I don't necessarily want three motors. I could do it but I would prefer to use one motor and just do them sequentially. That would add a little bit more complexity but I could do it with the 3D printer. Also, when this is in use it will primarily be used during sunrise or sunset so the amount of time it takes doesn't matter that much for it to rise or fall Attached 1 file. - 87364435-3a22-4203-9272-502fc4d0f4a2
turns.response_html:
This is a brilliant mechanical design challenge. Running three independent curtains off a single motor sequentially—meaning you can choose to lift curtain 1, then curtain 2, then curtain 3, or leave some down—adds an incredibly satisfying layer of mechanical complexity.

Since speed isn't a factor, you don't need a massive motor. You just need a way to selectively connect the motor's power to one of three different take-up spools.

Doing this with a 3D printer opens up two distinct architectural approaches: a Sliding Selector Key (linear selection) or a Rotational Dog Clutch (pivoting selection).

Approach 1: The Sliding "Key" Drive Shaft (Linear Selection)

Instead of moving gears physically in and out of mesh, you keep all three string spools sitting inline on a single, hollow or slotted main axle.

  • How the Spools Sit: The three spools are mounted on the axle with internal bearings or smooth bores so they can spin completely freely on their own. They don't turn when the motor turns unless they are locked in.
  • The Sliding Key: Inside the main axle (or running along a keyway slot on the outside), you print a solid "drive key" attached to a long push-pull rod.
  • How it works: 1. You push or pull the selector rod to a specific detent (Position 1, 2, or 3). 2. The key slides into the center core of Spool 2, mechanically locking that spool to the motor's drive shaft. 3. You turn on the DC motor. The axle spins, but only Spool 2 rotates to lift its curtain. Spool 1 and 3 stay completely still.
  • The Free-Fall Integration: You can include a "Neutral" position between the detents. When the key is parked in Neutral, you can press your ratchet release button, and that specific curtain will drop via gravity independently.

Approach 2: The Tilting Tumbler Gear (Rotational Selection)

If you prefer keeping the spools completely isolated on their own fixed pins, you can mount the DC motor on a printed pivoting arm (a tumbler assembly).

  • The Layout: The three spools are mounted side-by-side, each with a large gear printed onto its outer edge.
  • The Tumbler: The DC motor sits on a bracket that can rotate or slide laterally across the top of the window frame.
  • How it works:
    1. You physically slide or pivot the motor bracket until its main drive gear aligns and meshes with the gear of Curtain 3.
    2. You run the motor to lift it.
    3. The other two curtains are completely unmeshed. To keep them from falling while unmeshed, each individual spool retains its own independent gravity ratchet pawl.
    4. To drop a specific curtain, you just press the dedicated manual ratchet release lever for that window pane.

3D Printing Material & Tolerances

Because this setup relies on indexing and holding positions, choosing the right print settings on your printer is key:

  • For the Gears and Drive Keys: Use PETG or Nylon. If you use PLA, the repeated engagement of a sliding key or meshing gears will eventually cause the plastic teeth to shear or wear down into dust.
  • Perimeters and Infill: Print the structural selector components with at least 4 to 5 perimeters (walls) and a high infill density (40%+ Gyroid) to handle the rotational torsional stress of lifting the curtains with the bottom poles installed.

Approach 1 (the sliding internal key) keeps the entire footprint incredibly compact and streamlined right along the top header of the window frame, while Approach 2 (the tumbler gear) is highly visual and easier to troubleshoot mechanically.

Do you like the idea of a single selector rod you push/pull from the side to choose the window, or does a pivoting gear selector sound more robust for your layout?
